title: Mercy and sin (CCC 1846–1848)
hookLine: the gospel reveals mercy toward sinners

cards: Joseph is asleep, and troubled. The woman he's engaged to is pregnant, and the child isn't his. He's already decided to send her away quietly.
Then, Matthew says, an angel comes to him in a dream, tells him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife, and gives him the child's name before he's born.
In the Douay-Rheims: "thou shalt call his name JESUS. For he shall save his people from their sins." Before a single miracle or sermon, the name is about sin, and about rescue from it.

teach.h: THE GOSPEL REVEALS MERCY TO SINNERS.
teach.b: The Catechism starts its teaching on sin with that name, and with a sentence easy to miss: the Gospel is the revelation, in Jesus Christ, of God's mercy to sinners. Notice the order.
It doesn't begin with a catalog of wrongs and offer a way out at the end. It begins with mercy, and sin comes into view inside it.
The angel's words are its first witness; the second is the Last Supper, where Jesus calls the cup his blood, shed for the forgiveness of sins. Still, mercy isn't cheap.
It quotes Saint Augustine: God created us without us, but he did not will to save us without us. Mercy is offered, but it has to be received, and receiving it starts with honesty.

The first letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins."
So, in this teaching, the admission isn't the price of mercy. It's the open hand that takes it. Last, Paul: "where sin abounded, grace did more abound."
But grace, the Catechism says, has to uncover sin in order to heal it, and it borrows an image from Pope John Paul the Second: a physician who probes the wound before treating it. The probing hurts.

teach.h: WHERE SIN ABOUNDED, GRACE DID MORE ABOUND.
teach.b: It's also how a wound gets clean. In this teaching, nobody is asked to earn their way back before they're loved. Mercy is there first.

how: Catholics confess sins to God and, in the sacrament of penance, to a priest, who speaks words of absolution; the Church teaches that God's mercy is offered to every sinner who turns back.

o: God forgives only after you have paid for your sins
God's mercy comes first, and naming sin lets it in
sin is too small a thing for God to bother about

games.q: mercy and sin — tap the pairs.
p: probes the wound to heal it

the name comes in the dream, before the birth: he shall save his people from their sins.
in this teaching, a person must fix themselves before mercy is offered
mercy comes first; admitting sin is how it is received.

games.q: you're Joseph. your fiancée is pregnant, and the child isn't yours. you've decided to send her away quietly. then an angel speaks in a dream. what happens?
o: you send her away anyway, as planned.
you take her home and name the child as the angel said.
you wait for a second sign before deciding.
games.why: Joseph wakes and does as the angel commanded: he takes Mary as his wife, and the child is named Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've done that you keep carrying, and look at it plainly, without exaggerating it or explaining it away.

Say it to yourself in a single sentence; if you pray, say it to God, then try the harder part, loosening your grip on it. If you don't pray, notice what it would be like to put it down, and let your hands open on your lap.

wordCard.voice: Mercy and sin. The Catechism says the Gospel is God's mercy revealed to sinners: mercy comes first, and seeing sin honestly is how a person receives it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: mercy, pity — a New Testament word for God's mercy.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy first. Naming the wrong comes inside the mercy, not before it. Go gently.
